issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires an interest in disputed immovable property during a pending suit cannot claim an automatic right to be impleaded in that suit.
material_facts: A suit seeking specific performance and related relief concerning immovable property was pending.
Interests in the disputed property were transferred while the suit was pending and without the court’s permission.
The transferees applied to be added as parties and to file written statements; the trial court rejected the application, but the High Court allowed it.
issues.conclusion: The transferees could not seek impleadment as of right. The High Court’s order was set aside and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the doctrine of lis pendens. A pendente lite transferee is bound by the decree and is not, merely by acquiring an interest, entitled as of right to join the suit. Order I Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs addition of parties; Order XXII Rule 10 does not make it obligatory for a person acquiring an interest during litigation to seek leave to continue the suit. The Court relied on Sarvinder Singh v. Dalip Singh, Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University, and its discussion of Bibi Zubaida Khatoon v. Nabi Hassan Saheb, including the principle that there is no rule requiring such a transferee to contest every pending suit.

predicates.impleadment_application_in_pending_prope: A person who acquired an interest in disputed immovable property asks to be added to the pending suit concerning that property.
predicates.interest_acquired_during_suit: The person acquired the interest while the suit concerning the property was pending.
predicates.transfer_without_court_permission: The interest was transferred without the court’s authority or permission.

issues.definition: When a person seeks to join a pending property suit after acquiring an interest during the suit through a transfer made without court permission, that person has no automatic right to be added.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of an interest in disputed immovable property during a pending suit does not defeat the rights that may be established by the decree, regardless of the transferee’s good faith.
material_facts: The suit directly concerned rights in immovable property.
The property was transferred while the suit was pending, without the court’s permission, including through subsequent transfers to the applicants for impleadment.
issues.conclusion: The transfers were subject to the doctrine of lis pendens, and the transferees were bound by the decree as if they had been parties to the suit; good faith or bona fides did not alter that result.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that, during a non-collusive suit in which rights to immovable property are directly and specifically in question, a party cannot transfer or otherwise deal with the property so as to affect another party’s rights under a decree, except with court authority. The doctrine is one of public policy; the pendency of the suit does not prohibit a transfer, but the transfer cannot affect the rights established by the decree. A transferee pendente lite is bound by the decree. The Court relied on Sarvinder Singh v. Dalip Singh and Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University.

issues.definition: If an interest in property directly at issue in a pending non-collusive suit is transferred without court permission, the transferee remains bound by the decree.
